analysis.one_liner: Bars insurers from denying or limiting coverage to victims of domestic abuse.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar insurers from discriminating against domestic abuse victims was referred to three subcommittees in 1996 and never received a vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for insurance companies and employer health plans to deny someone coverage, cancel a policy, raise their premium, or refuse a claim because the person has been a victim of domestic abuse. It also would have limited how insurers could share information about a person's abuse history, required insurers to explain in writing why they took an adverse action on an abuse-related claim, and imposed fines of up to $25,000 per violation. It never advanced past subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of domestic violence. At the time, insurers could deny coverage, charge higher premiums, or refuse claims for injuries linked to abuse — treating being a victim as a pre-existing risk. The bill would have ended that practice, guaranteed continued coverage for someone leaving an abuser's policy, kept abuse-related information from circulating among insurers, and required written explanations for adverse decisions. All policyholders also benefit from not having a victim's private medical history used as underwriting data.

how_it_helps.text: It barred insurers and group health plans from denying, canceling, or restricting coverage, or raising premiums, because a person is, has been, or may be a victim of domestic abuse [S2, S3].

It stopped insurers from denying claims for injuries caused by domestic abuse, and required written explanations for any adverse action on a claim the insurer knows or should know is abuse-related [S2, S3].

It protected victims' privacy by limiting how insurers could use or share information about a person's abuse status, and barred insurers from pursuing subrogation (going after an abuser's assets to recover claim costs) without the victim's informed consent — protecting victims from actions that could provoke retaliation [S3].

It required insurers to file safety protocols for handling insurance actions that could endanger a victim, and set up state enforcement with a federal fallback and civil money penalties up to $25,000 per violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies — health, life, disability, and property/casualty insurers — would have lost the ability to price or deny coverage based on abuse history, absorbed new compliance and paperwork costs, and faced civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation in states without approved enforcement programs.

drawbacks.text: It added new federal regulation of the insurance industry, touching all lines of insurance, with federal civil money penalties up to $25,000 per violation in states without an approved regulatory program [S3].

It gave the federal government a role in traditionally state-regulated insurance, including federal fallback standards if the National Association of Insurance Commissioners did not act within 90 days — a genuine jurisdictional objection a good-faith opponent could raise [S3].

Even under the bill, victims' protections had limits: insurers could still require abuse survivors to pay the full premium to keep coverage after leaving an abuser's policy, and could still deny life insurance when the applicant was an abuser with an insurable-interest problem [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for a vulnerable group were real and the costs modest: insurers would forgo the ability to price or deny based on abuse history, and would bear administrative costs for protocols and written explanations. The bill was carefully limited (it allowed insurers to require full premium payment and to deny life insurance to abusers, and it let industry self-regulate via the NAIC before any federal standard applied). An honest supporter would acknowledge it added federal rules to a state-regulated industry and some compliance burden; an honest critic would struggle to name a public cost. The real flaw was not design but fate: it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to House committees and then to three subcommittees, none of which acted on it before Congress adjourned in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 5, 1996, and referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities [S1, S5].
Within about two weeks it was referred to three subcommittees — Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials; Health and Environment; and Employer-Employee Relations — where it sat [S5].
No further action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill never received a committee markup or a House vote [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry kept the ability to underwrite based on abuse history without federal penalty; no one else gained.

for.name: Rep. Earl Pomeroy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 5, 1996, and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1, S5].

for.name: 22 House cosponsors (21 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

against.name: House Commerce and Education & Workforce subcommittees
against.role: Subcommittees on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials; Health and Environment; and Employer-Employee Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 14 and 21, 1996, and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committees never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Health, life, disability, and property/casualty insurers
industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from denying coverage, denying claims, or raising premiums based on domestic abuse status, restricted their use of abuse-related information, and exposed them to civil penalties. Insurers would lose a (narrow) underwriting tool in exchange for new compliance duties.

industries.industry: Health maintenance organizations and group health plans
industries.note: HMOs and employer group health plans would face the same anti-discrimination and privacy limits, enforced by the Labor Department under ERISA. Their interest in denying abuse-related claims ran against victims' access to care.
Employers sponsoring group health plans would face new federal compliance obligations, though modest ones, to keep coverage available to employees fleeing abuse.
